title: Castle only after checking the king’s route
goal: Know the two-piece castling move and test the conditions that make it legal.
opening: Castling moves the king and one rook in a single turn. Kingside castling takes White’s king from e1 to g1 and rook from h1 to f1. The king moves two squares toward the rook; the rook lands beside it on the other side.

You cannot use this move whenever the destination looks comfortable. The king and that rook must not have moved before, the squares between them must be empty, and the king cannot start in check, cross an attacked square, or finish on an attacked square.
heading: Inspect where the king starts, passes and finishes
teaching: For White’s kingside castle, inspect e1, f1 and g1. If e1 is attacked, castling is not an answer to the check. If f1 is attacked, the king cannot cross it even when g1 is safe. If g1 is attacked, the king cannot finish there. The rook’s starting square may be attacked without itself forbidding castling; the special attack restrictions concern the king’s route.

The position diagram does not always reveal the move history. A king that moved away and returned to e1 has lost castling rights. The same applies to the rook used. Our worked positions state that the rights are available, so you can focus on the empty path and attacks. In a real game, remember what moved earlier rather than judging only the current arrangement.

Queenside castling follows the same idea: White’s king goes e1 to c1 and rook a1 to d1. The intervening b1, c1 and d1 must be empty, but the king’s attack checks are on e1, d1 and c1. Do not mistakenly require b1 to be unattacked merely because it lies between rook and king.
terms: The historical permission retained only if the relevant king and rook have not moved.

first.title: A clear, safe kingside route
first.problem: White has Ke1 and Rh1, with castling rights; Black has Ke8. All other squares are empty. Can White castle kingside?
steps: Check history and space
The rights are stated; f1 and g1 are empty.
Without the stated rights, the diagram alone would not settle the history.
Check attacks
Black’s king on e8 attacks none of e1, f1 or g1.
These are the king’s start, crossing and finishing squares.
Make both parts of the move
O-O: king e1→g1, rook h1→f1.
This is one move, not a king move followed by an extra turn.
first.notice: Castling is legal here because every required condition is satisfied.

second.title: A safe destination is not enough
second.problem: Add a black rook on f8 to the same position. The f-file is otherwise clear. Can White still castle kingside?
steps: Find the rook’s attack
Rf8 attacks f1 down the open file.
White’s king on e1 is not currently in that line.
Inspect the crossing square
The king would have to pass through f1.
An attacked crossing square forbids castling.
Reject the castle
O-O is illegal in this position.
A safe-looking g1 does not compensate for crossing an attacked f1.
second.notice: Do not move the king through check while checking only its final square.

exercise: A king moved from e1 earlier and returned. Its route is now clear and safe. May it castle?
No. The king has already moved and lost castling rights. A clear current diagram cannot restore those rights.

title: Tell a king pin from a pin to a valuable piece
goal: Distinguish an illegal move that exposes the king from a legal move that exposes another target.
opening: A piece can stand between an attacker and something behind it. Moving that piece may uncover the attack. This arrangement is called a pin, but the rules depend on what is behind the piece.
If the target behind it is the king, a move exposing that king to check is illegal. If the target is a queen, the move may be legal but costly. Those are different reasons for a piece to stay put.
heading: Look all the way down the line
teaching: White’s bishop on c3 points along d4, e5, f6 and g7. Put a black knight on f6 and black king on g7. The knight blocks the bishop’s line. If the knight moves off that line, the bishop attacks the king. In the stated position the knight has no legal jump that removes it from the line while leaving its king safe. That is an absolute pin.

For a relative pin, put White’s rook on d1, Black’s knight on d7 and queen on d8, with the black king safely on a8. The knight blocks the rook’s route to the queen. Black can legally play Nf6 because the move does not expose the king. White can then play Rxd8+ and capture the queen. The word pinned described a tactical cost, not a prohibition in the movement rules.

A pin does not automatically win a piece. The attacker may itself be vulnerable, the defender may move the king off the line, or a forcing reply may matter more. Inspect a concrete continuation before turning the pattern into a conclusion about material.
terms: A line in which moving the intervening piece would illegally expose its king.
A line toward another valuable target; moving may still be legal.

first.title: The knight shields its own king
first.problem: White: Kg1, Bc3. Black: Kg7, Nf6. Black to move. Why can the knight not simply jump away?
steps: Trace the bishop
The knight is between bishop and king.
Remove the knight in your mental picture
The bishop would attack g7.
The move would leave Black’s king in check.
Apply the legality test
A knight move that exposes that attack is illegal.
Being able to make a two-and-one jump is not the whole legal-move test.
first.notice: The king behind the piece makes the restriction a rule of legality.

second.title: The queen is the target behind it
second.problem: White: Kg1, Rd1. Black: Ka8, Qd8, Nd7. Black plays Nf6. What can White do?
steps: Check that Black’s move is legal
Nd7–f6 does not expose the king on a8.
The rook’s line is on the d-file, not the king’s file.
Use the uncovered line
Rxd8+ captures the queen.
The d-file is now clear between White’s rook and d8.
Name the distinction
This was a relative pin, not an absolute one.
Black could move the knight legally, but that did not make the move a good choice.
second.notice: Legal and wise are separate judgments.

exercise: Why is pinned an incomplete explanation for saying a move is illegal?
You must identify what moving the piece exposes. Exposing one’s own king to check makes the move illegal; exposing a queen may make it costly while still legal.

title: Read the opponent’s last move before choosing yours
goal: Notice checks and attacked pieces, then verify a response on the resulting board.
opening: It is easy to spend a turn planning your own attack while overlooking what the opponent just changed. Before looking for something clever, ask whether your king is checked and whether a piece is newly attacked.

The first question has priority. If the king is in check, the next move must remove it. If there is no check, you have more freedom to compare captures, defenses and moves that take a threatened piece out of danger.
heading: Do not stop the search at the first attacked piece
teaching: White has king h1 and rook a1; Black has king h8 and bishop d4. Follow the bishop’s diagonal d4–c3–b2–a1. It attacks the rook. Follow its other diagonal through e3, f2 and g1: it does not attack the king on h1. White therefore has time to address the rook threat. Ra2 moves it off the attacked diagonal in this sparse position.

After choosing Ra2, inspect the new square. The bishop on d4 does not attack a2, and the distant king does not either. That makes the move a legal way to preserve the rook here. It does not establish that Ra2 is the only sensible move. A check, capture or different rook move could also deserve consideration in another position.

Use a short routine rather than scanning randomly: king safety first, then the opponent’s direct threats, then your candidates and the reply to each. The routine should end with the resulting board. A move that looked attractive from the starting diagram can fail once your piece leaves a defensive square.
terms: An action the opponent could profitably make on a coming move.
A possible move selected for closer examination.

first.title: Save an attacked rook without inventing a check
first.problem: White: Kh1, Ra1. Black: Kh8, Bd4. White to move. Show one legal way to move the rook out of attack.
steps: Locate the attack
Bd4 attacks a1 through c3 and b2.
Those intermediate squares are empty.
Check the king first
Kh1 is not attacked by the bishop or king.
White is not required to answer a check in this position.
Show one response
Ra2.
The rook leaves the bishop’s diagonal and lands on a safe square in the stated position.
first.notice: Identify the actual threat before choosing a response.

second.title: If the king is checked, priorities change
second.problem: Return to White Ke1, Bc1 and Black Ka8, Re8. Could White ignore the e-file to make an unrelated improving move?
steps: Confirm check
Re8 has a clear line to Ke1.
This is an immediate legal constraint, not merely a future threat.
Test the proposed result
If the e-file stays clear and the king stays on e1, the check remains.
An unrelated useful-looking move cannot make that legal.
Choose an actual answer
Be3 blocks the line; Kf1 is another legal reply in this four-piece position.
Check every enemy attack after choosing either move.
second.notice: A check is not just one item in a list of plans; it restricts which moves are allowed.

exercise: What two questions would you ask before carrying out your own planned attack?
First, is my king in check? Then, what direct threats did the opponent create, including attacked pieces? Any candidate still needs its resulting king safety and the opponent’s reply checked.

title: Promote a pawn—and inspect the position afterward
goal: Apply promotion correctly and recognize why queen promotion is not an automatic answer in every position.
opening: A white pawn reaching the eighth rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight of the same color as part of that move. A black pawn promotes on the first rank. You do not need to have lost the chosen piece earlier.
A queen is usually a strong choice because it combines rook and bishop movement. But choose by looking at the resulting board. A stronger-looking piece can accidentally leave the opponent stalemated.
heading: Promotion changes the attacks immediately
teaching: With White king c6 and pawn e6 against Black king a7, White can play e7. After one legal reply, ...Kb8, e8=Q+ promotes with check: the new queen on e8 attacks the king along the eighth rank. The pawn did not remain a pawn for an extra turn before acquiring the queen’s movement.

Now use White Kc6, Pc7 and Black Ka7, with White to move. After c8=Q, the black king is not in check. Yet a8 and b8 are covered by the queen, b7 and b6 by White’s king, and a6 by the queen’s diagonal. Black has no legal move: stalemate. Promoting to a rook instead leaves a6 available. This does not by itself teach a full winning method with king and rook; it shows why you must inspect the immediate result rather than always choose queen by habit.
The same legality check applies before the pawn push: your own king must remain safe. Promotion is a special result of a legal pawn move, not permission to ignore a check elsewhere.
terms: The pawn moves to e8, promotes to a queen and gives check.
Choosing a rook, bishop or knight instead of a queen.

first.title: The queen exists as soon as the pawn arrives
first.problem: White Kc6, Pe6; Black Ka7. Follow e7, ...Kb8, e8=Q+.
steps: Advance legally
The pawn moves forward to the empty square.
Show Black’s reply
This is one legal reply in the stated position.
Promote on arrival
Replace the pawn by a queen immediately; the new queen checks along the eighth rank.
first.notice: The chosen piece’s attacks count in the resulting position right away.

second.title: A queen can produce a draw by stalemate
second.problem: White Kc6, Pc7; Black Ka7. Compare c8=Q with c8=R.
steps: Inspect queen promotion
After c8=Q, Ka7 is not in check.
The queen on c8 does not attack a7.
Check the escapes
All neighboring squares are attacked, and Black has no other piece.
No check plus no legal move is stalemate.
Compare a rook
After c8=R, a6 is available to the black king.
The rook does not attack a6 diagonally. The immediate position is not stalemate.
second.notice: Underpromotion can change the legal replies; stronger material is not the only concern.

exercise: Why is checking only the value of the promoted piece insufficient?
The new attacks can change whether the opponent is checked, mated or stalemated. Inspect the king’s current square and every legal reply before choosing a promotion.

title: Build a mating net without confusing it with stalemate
goal: Verify a concrete queen-and-king mate and compare the nearby stalemate position.
opening: White’s king is on c6 and queen on b6; Black’s king is on a8. With White to move, Qb7 is checkmate in this small position. We will verify the attack and each escape instead of trusting how trapped the king looks.
The queen needs help from her king. On b7 she attacks a8, while the king on c6 protects b7. That protection is why Black cannot simply capture the checking queen.
heading: Check the current square and each destination separately
teaching: After Qb7+, the black king’s neighboring squares are a7, b7 and b8. The queen covers a7 along the seventh rank and b8 along the b-file. B7 contains the queen, but White’s king on c6 protects it. Capturing onto b7 would put the black king next to that enemy king and is illegal. There are no other black pieces to block or capture. Check plus no legal reply makes this mate.

Compare the original arrangement with Black to move: Ka8 against Kc6 and Qb6. The queen on b6 covers a7 diagonally and b7/b8 along the b-file, while the white king helps cover the neighboring area. Black has no legal move, but a8 is not attacked. The result is stalemate, not mate. Moving the queen from b6 to b7 changes the attack on the current king square, which changes a draw into a win in this example.

This position teaches how to verify a net. It is not a complete algorithm for mating from every queen-and-king position. In a longer ending you must still bring your king closer, preserve safe space for the opponent when it is their turn, and check each move’s result.
terms: An arrangement of attacks that leaves a checked king without a legal escape.
A checking piece that cannot simply be captured because its square is defended.

first.title: Prove that Qb7 is mate
first.problem: White Kc6, Qb6; Black Ka8. White to move. Follow Qb7#.
steps: Give check
Qb7 attacks a8 diagonally.
The king’s current square is attacked, so this is not stalemate.
Inspect a7 and b8
The queen attacks both.
The king cannot move onto either square.
Inspect capture on b7
White’s king on c6 protects b7.
Black cannot capture the queen there.
Finish the test
No legal reply remains: checkmate.
The conclusion follows from the actual attacks, not the queen’s material value.
first.notice: A mate claim deserves a complete reply search, even in a tiny position.

second.title: The nearby stalemate
second.problem: Use the original Kc6, Qb6 versus Ka8 position, but give Black the move.
steps: Inspect a8
The queen on b6 does not attack it.
Black is not checked.
Inspect all moves
a7, b7 and b8 are attacked.
The king has no legal destination, and Black has no other piece.
Name the result
Stalemate: a draw.
The absence of check changes the result.
second.notice: Trapped is not a sufficient chess result. You must know whether the king is attacked.

exercise: Why can Black not answer Qb7+ by capturing the queen?
The queen on b7 is protected by White’s king on c6. A black king on b7 would be attacked by that king, so Kxb7 is illegal.

title: Replay a short game and find the missed threat
goal: Follow both sides of a miniature game and explain a legal defense before the mating move.
opening: A short mating pattern can be useful to study without becoming a trick you try blindly. Here White’s queen and bishop converge on f7. Watch how Black’s reply either allows that attack or addresses it.
The line is 1 e4 e5 2 Bc4 Nc6 3 Qh5 Nf6? 4 Qxf7#. The question mark marks a poor move in this position, not an illegal one. We will compare it with a different response to the queen.
heading: Developing a piece does not excuse ignoring a threat
teaching: After Bc4 and Qh5, both White pieces attack f7. Black’s ...Nf6 develops the knight and attacks the queen on h5, but White is not required to save the queen if a stronger move finishes the game. Qxf7 captures the pawn with check. The queen on f7 is protected by the bishop on c4, so the black king cannot take it. The remaining replies do not remove the check; the board shows mate.

Before that mistake, ...g6 is one legal way to challenge the queen and block the h5–g6–f7 diagonal. White can retreat with Qf3, after which ...Nf6 develops while also interrupting the queen’s f-file line to f7. This is a worked defense, not a claim that it is the only good response or a complete opening repertoire. Its value is showing that the exact position and threat matter more than the slogan develop a knight.

When replaying the game, pause after each move and describe one changed attack or opened line. If you cannot explain why the last move mattered, use the board’s previous-move control. Reading an annotated game should connect moves to consequences, rather than turn into a recital of notation.
terms: An annotation marking a questionable or poor move, rather than an illegality.
Queen captures on f7 and checkmates.
A short game, used here as a compact teaching example.

first.title: The unaddressed attack on f7
first.problem: Follow 1 e4 e5 2 Bc4 Nc6 3 Qh5 Nf6? 4 Qxf7#.
steps: Find the shared target
Bc4 and Qh5 both point toward f7.
Trace each line rather than only looking at the king.
Inspect Black’s reply
...Nf6 attacks the queen but leaves the mating threat available.
A threat against the queen is not automatically the most urgent event.
Play the finish
Qxf7#.
The bishop protects the queen; Black cannot legally capture it with the king.
Verify, do not memorize only
Check the king’s possible destinations and other replies.
The independent move rules confirm mate in this exact line.
first.notice: A legal developing move can still lose immediately if it ignores a stronger threat.

second.title: Answer the threat before it lands
second.problem: Return to the position after 3 Qh5 and follow ...g6, Qf3, ...Nf6.
steps: Interrupt the diagonal
...g6 occupies g6 and attacks Qh5.
The queen’s route to f7 is no longer the same.
Show White’s retreat
Qf3.
The queen moves along h5–g4–f3.
Develop with a defensive job
The knight now blocks the queen’s f-file line toward f7 as well as entering play.
second.notice: The same-looking developing move must be evaluated in the position where it is actually played.

exercise: Why did attacking the queen with ...Nf6 fail in the first line?

White had the stronger immediate reply Qxf7#. The queen captured with mate and did not need to retreat from the knight’s attack. Check the opponent’s forcing possibilities before assuming your threat must be answered.
